title: Alcohols
learningObjective: know that alcohols contain the functional group −OH; understand how to draw structural and displayed formulae for methanol, ethanol, propanol (propan-1-ol only) and butanol (butan-1-ol only), and name each compound the names propanol and butanol are acceptable; know that ethanol can be oxidised by: • burning in air or oxygen (complete combustion) • reaction with oxygen in the air to form ethanoic acid (microbial oxidation) • heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid to form ethanoic acid; know that ethanol can be manufactured by: • reacting ethene with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst at a temperature of about 300 ºC and a pressure of about 60–70 atm • the fermentation of glucose, in the absence of air, at an optimum temperature of about 30 ºC and using the enzymes in yeast; understand the reasons for fermentation, in the absence of air, and at an optimum temperature

sections.title: Alcohols
sections.markdown:
The word "alcohol" in everyday speech means one specific liquid —
but in chemistry it names an entire family. **[[alcohol]]s** are an
important class of organic compounds: a **[[homologous-series]]**
whose members all carry the **–OH functional group** covalently
bonded to a carbon chain. What people commonly call "alcohol" is
just one member of that family — the drink industry's ethanol —
and even that molecule should properly be called
**[[ethanol]]**, C₂H₅OH, or better, showing the structure,
CH₃CH₂OH. Every chemistry idea you already own from the organic
chapters — formula types, series behaviour, the reactivity that a
[[functional-group]] confers — transfers directly to this family;
the –OH group simply replaces the C=C handle of the alkenes
(u4:c25) as the reactive site everything else happens at.

The family is small at this level and its chemistry is organised
around one member. You will draw and name the first four alcohols,
then watch ethanol — the family's representative — do three
characteristic things: burn, oxidise to ethanoic acid (three
different ways, one of them in a wine bottle), and get manufactured
industrially by two competing routes whose trade-offs the
comparison section sets side by side. Every specification statement
of this chapter — 4.29C to 4.33C — is chemistry-only content,
assessed in Paper 2C alone, so this lesson is paper-2 territory
through and through.

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter builds directly on the hydration of ethene you met in
the previous lesson (u4:c25) — ethanol's industrial route in — and
on the organic toolkit from the introduction (u4:c22): homologous
series, functional groups, isomerism, formula types. The –OH
group's covalent O–H bond leans on the covalent bonding model
(u1:c08), and the combustion equation in Section 3 reuses the
balancing discipline from the formulae chapters (u1:c05).
:::

:::exam-hint
The functional group of the alcohols is the **–OH (hydroxyl)
group**. Write it with the dash: –OH, "covalently bonded to a
carbon chain" when the question asks for the full statement
(4.29C). Do not write just "O" or "H" — and do not confuse the
family name (alcohols) with the one member everyone has heard of
(ethanol).
:::

:::misconception
"'Alcohol' is a single substance." It is a family — a homologous
series — of which ethanol is merely the most familiar member.
Methanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol are all alcohols too, with
the same –OH group and their own properties; the drinks-cabinet
meaning of the word is a chemistry accident, not a definition.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the alcohol functional group as –OH? Can you say why
ethanol is the proper name for the "alcohol" of everyday speech?
Can you name the four alcohols this chapter covers? Then the
family portrait is hung — move on to drawing it.
:::

sections.title: Drawing and naming the alcohols
sections.markdown:
Four alcohols cover the whole requirement: **[[methanol]]**,
**ethanol**, **propan-1-ol** and **butan-1-ol**. Their formulae
line up below — read the columns exactly as you read the alkane
and alkene tables, because the skill is the same one at a new
functional group.

| Name | Molecular formula | Structural formula |
|------|-------------------|--------------------|
| methanol | CH₄O | CH₃OH |
| ethanol | C₂H₆O | CH₃CH₂OH |
| propan-1-ol | C₃H₈O | CH₃CH₂CH₂OH |
| butan-1-ol | C₄H₁₀O | CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH |

Each molecule can also be drawn as a **[[displayed-formula]]**,
and the alcohol version has one discipline the hydrocarbon tables
never needed: the O–H bond must be shown explicitly. Methanol's
displayed formula is a central C bonded to three H atoms and to an
O, with the O bonded to one more H (the O–H); ethanol extends the
carbon chain by one carbon before the –OH; propan-1-ol and
butan-1-ol extend it further, with the –OH always on the end
carbon. Draw every bond as a line and every atom as a symbol, and
check that each carbon shows four bonds and the oxygen shows two.

The naming code decodes in three slices. The 'meth', 'eth',
'prop' and 'but' parts count the carbon atoms; the 'an' part says
the chain is saturated with no carbon-carbon double bonds; the
'ol' announces the –OH functional group. **Propanol** and
**butanol** are acceptable names in the exam — you do not need the
locant number for full credit — but you must understand it, because
the number tells you *where* the –OH group sits. Counting from the
end that gives the smaller number: –OH on the end carbon gives
propan-**1**-ol; –OH on the middle carbon gives propan-**2**-ol.

That positional freedom generates **[[isomer]]s** again: propan-1-ol
and propan-2-ol share one [[molecular-formula]] but differ in
structure, and the same holds for butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol. The
numbering convention from the alkene chapter (u4:c25) carries over
unchanged — smallest locant wins.

For the rest of this chapter, ethanol stands in for the whole
family: one molecule, three characteristic reactions, two
industrial routes.

:::exam-hint
Two drawing rules earn or lose the mark. First, when drawing the
displayed formula of any alcohol you **must show the bond between
the O and the H** — write the O–H explicitly; an oxygen left
hanging with no H is the classic lost mark. Second, the names
**propanol and butanol are acceptable in the exam** —
but if the question names propan-1-ol and you draw the –OH on a
middle carbon, the drawing is wrong no matter how tidy it is.
:::

:::key-point
The alcohol name decode: prefix counts the carbons (meth, eth,
prop, but), infix '-an-' certifies single bonds only, suffix
'-ol' flags the –OH group. The locant number in propan-1-ol
reports which carbon carries the –OH, counted from the end that
gives the smaller number.
:::

:::misconception
"Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are the same compound with the –OH
drawn at different places for convenience." Different placement of
the functional group means a genuinely different compound — the
defining test of an [[isomer]] pair — with different properties
and (at A level) different chemistry. The locant is structural
information, not a drawing convention.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the molecular and structural formulae of all four
alcohols from memory? Can you draw ethanol's displayed formula
with the O–H bond shown and every bond accounted for? Can you
explain what the 1 in propan-1-ol reports, and name the isomer it
hides? Four yeses and 4.30C is banked.
:::

sections.title: Ethanol burns in air
sections.markdown:
The first of ethanol's three oxidations is the oldest one:
combustion. All alcohols burn to form carbon dioxide and water —
the same [[complete-combustion]] products as every hydrocarbon,
plus nothing new, because the –OH group's oxygen simply joins the
oxygen accounting. With ethanol:

C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)

Balance it once slowly: carbons 2 = 2; hydrogens 6 = 6; oxygens
1 + 6 = 7 on the left and 4 + 3 = 7 on the right. The odd-looking
coefficient distribution — the same 3 serving both O₂ and H₂O —
is what the extra oxygen atom in the alcohol does to the arithmetic.

What makes this combustion worth a section of its own is where the
ethanol comes from. Ethanol is a **[[biofuel]]**: a fuel made from
biological sources such as sugar cane or corn, rather than from
crude oil. Mixtures of petrol with ethanol are increasingly used in
countries such as Brazil, which have little or no oil industry of
their own but a climate that grows sugar cane superbly. Other
countries are introducing biofuels such as ethanol to reduce
dependence on **fossil fuels, which are finite non-renewable
resources** — burn them and there are no more. The fuel itself is
ordinary combustion chemistry; the strategic point is the source of
the carbon.

:::did-you-know
Brazil's petrol pumps dispense the chemistry of this section at
national scale: sugarcane ethanol blended into petrol, a fleet
running partly on this year's harvest instead of hundred-million-
year-old oil. The same equation — C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O —
powers both a laboratory spirit lamp and a national fuel policy.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The biofuel story is a geography-and-economics case study wearing
a chemistry equation. Geography sets the stage: sugar cane needs
the tropical climate Brazil has and crude oil fields it lacks, so
the map of fuel production follows the climate zones, not the
geology. Economics supplies the motive: ethanol blends cut oil
imports and build energy independence, while the finiteness of
fossil reserves makes the renewable route a long-run strategy
rather than a fashion. The comparison section (Section 8) puts
numbers on the trade-off.
:::

:::exam-hint
The combustion-of-ethanol equation is a favourite one-mark
derivation because the oxygen in the –OH trips people up. Derive
in the fixed order — hydrogens to water first, carbons second,
oxygen last — and the (l) state symbol on the ethanol (it is a
liquid fuel) comes free with the working. Statement 4.31C wants
this as the *first* oxidation route: burning in air or oxygen.
:::

:::misconception
"Biofuels contain no carbon because they are 'green'." Ethanol
burns to carbon dioxide exactly like every other fuel — the –OH
group changes nothing about the products. What biofuel changes is
the *source* of the carbon (recent biological growth rather than
fossil deposits) and the renewability of the supply. Products:
CO₂ and H₂O, always.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write and balance the complete-combustion equation for
ethanol, with state symbols? Can you define a biofuel and say why
Brazil leads the way? Can you name the property fossil fuels have
that biofuels renewably replace — finiteness? Three yeses and the
first oxidation is yours.
:::

sections.title: Microbial oxidation
sections.markdown:
The second oxidation needs no flame and no laboratory: air and
microbes do it. Ethanol is oxidised by the air **in the presence of
microbes** — bacteria or yeast — and the product is
**[[ethanoic-acid]]**, CH₃COOH. This is **[[microbial-oxidation]]**,
and you have almost certainly watched it happen: a bottle of wine
left open to the air turns sour. The French for sour wine is *vin
aigre*, which over the centuries has been distorted into
**vinegar** — the word on the label is a record of this reaction.

Ethanoic acid is the family's first look at the carboxylic acids —
a later chapter (u4:c27) takes that family properly.
What matters here is the transformation: ethanol's –OH carbon gains
a bond to oxygen, and the –CH₂CH₃ end of the molecule becomes the
–COOH (carboxylic acid) group. Drawn as displayed formulae, ethanol
and ethanoic acid sit side by side with exactly two extra oxygen
bonds marking the oxidation.

Statement 4.31C lists this route in its own words — *reaction with
oxygen in the air to form ethanoic acid (microbial oxidation)* —
so learn the phrase "microbial oxidation" as the name of the route,
with wine-turning-to-vinegar as its everyday evidence.

:::did-you-know
The old name for ethanoic acid was **acetic acid** — from the same
Latin *acetum* (sour) that gives vinegar its logic in both
languages. When you meet "acetic" on old bottles or in older
textbooks, it is this molecule: CH₃COOH, the oxidation product of
ethanol, wearing its historical name.
:::

:::exam-hint
For "ethanol is oxidised by the air", the mark scheme wants the
microbe credited: **oxidised by oxygen in the air with the help of
microorganisms (bacteria or yeast) to form ethanoic acid,
CH₃COOH**. Writing only "it turns to vinegar" describes the
evidence but misses the chemistry — name the product and the
agents (air + microbes), and the marks follow.
:::

:::misconception
"Wine turns sour because air oxidises the ethanol directly, no
living help needed." The air supplies the oxidant, but the
reaction needs the microbes' help — bacteria or yeast are the
workers, which is why the route is named *microbial* oxidation.
Sterile conditions slow it dramatically; the open bottle goes
sour because the microbial workforce is everywhere.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you name the second oxidation route in 4.31C's own words? Can
you write the formula of ethanoic acid and say which family it
belongs to? Can you tell the wine-to-vinegar story with the
chemistry in it? Three yeses and the gentlest oxidation is done.
:::

sections.title: Lab oxidation with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
sections.markdown:
The third oxidation is the one you can run yourself, and it is the
usual way of oxidising ethanol (and other alcohols) in the lab. The
**[[oxidising-agent]]** is a mixture of **potassium dichromate(VI)**
and **dilute sulfuric acid**. Potassium dichromate(VI) is a strong
oxidising agent with the formula K₂Cr₂O₇, and the dilute sulfuric
acid matters more than it looks: without the H⁺ ions from the acid,
no redox reaction will occur — the acid is a working partner, not a
spectator.

The procedure is a two-tube story in one test-tube. A few drops of
ethanol are added to a solution containing the **orange** mixture of
potassium dichromate(VI) and dilute sulfuric acid; the tube is
heated in a hot water bath; the solution turns **green**, and now
contains a very dilute solution of [[ethanoic-acid]] together with
other products. The green colour indicates the presence of Cr³⁺
ions, formed when the potassium dichromate(VI) is *reduced* —
orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ goes in, green Cr³⁺ comes out, and the ethanol pays
for it by being oxidised.

The full equation for this reaction is very complicated, so organic
chemistry uses a shorthand: the oxidising agent is written as
**[O]** in equations. Reading the [O] as "one oxygen atom delivered
by the oxidising agent", the reaction becomes clean:

CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O

Balance-check it: carbons 2 = 2; hydrogens 6 = 4 + 2 ✓; oxygens
1 + 2 = 3 on the left and 2 + 1 = 3 on the right. Two [O] units
take ethanol to ethanoic acid, with water as the co-product.

The reaction is run under **[[reflux]]**: heating with a condenser
placed vertically in the top of the flask, so that any vapours
condense and run back instead of escaping. Reflux keeps the
volatile ethanol in the reaction long enough to be fully oxidised.
You can even make a sample of pure-ish ethanoic acid this way:
heat ethanol with an *excess* of the oxidising agent under reflux,
then rearrange the condenser for a simple distillation — ethanoic
acid and water distil over together and are collected as a
solution.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and add the reactants very slowly — too
violent a reaction is possible. Never point the mouth of the
test-tube towards you: the contents may 'spit' out.
:::

:::exam-hint
The dichromate oxidation answer set: reagents (**potassium
dichromate(VI) and dilute sulfuric acid**), conditions (**heat
under reflux**), observation (**orange to green**), product
(**ethanoic acid**), and the equation with **[O]** standing in for
the oxidising agent. The (VI) in the name is not decoration —
other chromates exist that cannot oxidise alcohols, so the
statement 4.31C route is *dichromate(VI)* specifically. The
naming detail ('di-' = two chromium atoms; the roman numeral
reporting how the ion's charges and oxidation states work, met
with Cu(II) and Fe(III) in the ionic bonding chapter, u1:c07) is
extension territory — the oxidation state concept itself is not
required at International GCSE.
:::

:::misconception
"[O] is a real species — the equation shows an oxygen atom flying
around on its own." [O] is bookkeeping, not chemistry: a shorthand
for "one oxygen atom delivered by the oxidising agent", used
because the true dichromate equation is too complicated for this
course. Write it exactly as the convention — 2[O], square
brackets — and describe the oxidising agent by name in prose
(dichromate(VI)/acid), never as a free oxygen atom.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you name the reagent pair and the condition (reflux)? Can you
state the colour change and explain what the green colour tells
you about the dichromate? Can you write the [O] equation and
balance it by counting [O] units? Can you say why the acid is
essential? Four yeses and the lab oxidation is exam-ready.
:::

sections.title: Making ethanol by fermentation
sections.markdown:
Industry makes ethanol two ways, and the first is older than
chemistry itself: **[[fermentation]]**. **[[yeast]]** is added to a
sugar (or starch) solution and left in the warm — about 30 °C — for
several days **in the absence of air** ([[anaerobic]] conditions).
**[[enzyme]]s** (biological catalysts) in the yeast convert the
sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Starting from [[glucose]], the
overall conversion is:

C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g)

One glucose molecule, two ethanol molecules, two carbon dioxides —
and no help from heat, pressure or an industrial catalyst, because
the enzymes do the work at room-warm temperatures.

The conditions are not preferences; they are requirements, and
statement 4.33C asks you to *explain* them. **Why the absence of
air?** In the presence of air (aerobic conditions), the enzymes in
the yeast produce carbon dioxide and water *instead of* ethanol —
the same biochemical machinery, a completely different product.
Anaerobic conditions force the glucose down the ethanol pathway.
**Why the temperature?** The enzymes are protein catalysts: if the
temperature rises much above 40 °C they lose their structure and
stop working — the proteins are said to be **denatured**. At a
lower temperature the reaction is simply too slow. Somewhere
between 30 and 40 °C is the optimum: fast enough to be useful,
gentle enough to keep the proteins folded.

The biochemistry underneath is more complicated than the overall
equation suggests — ordinary sugar (sucrose) is first split by
water into two smaller sugars, glucose and fructose, which are
structural isomers sharing the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆, and the
yeast's enzymes then convert the glucose to ethanol in many small
steps. The sucrose hydrolysis that opens the sequence:

C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁(aq) + H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + C₆H₁₂O₆(aq)

Fermentation's industrial wrapper: raw material glucose (from
sugar cane, maize/corn, wheat and other starchy materials),
temperature 30 °C, catalyst enzymes in yeast, other conditions
anaerobic. And one hard ceiling: yeast is killed by more than
about 15% of alcohol in the mixture, so it is impossible to make
pure alcohol by fermentation — the ethanol must afterwards be
purified by fractional distillation, which takes advantage of the
boiling-point gap between ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C). The
fractional-distillation technique itself was met earlier in the
course (u1:c02).

:::key-point
Fermentation: yeast + sugar solution, warm (~30 °C), several days,
in the absence of air. Enzymes in the yeast convert glucose into
ethanol and carbon dioxide. No air — because with air the enzymes
make CO₂ and water instead — and no more than ~40 °C — because
the protein enzymes denature above it.
:::

:::exam-hint
4.33C is an *explain* statement, so give mechanisms, not
adjectives. Absence of air: **with air (aerobic conditions) the
enzymes produce carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol**.
Temperature between 30 and 40 °C: **enzymes are proteins; above
about 40 °C they denature (lose their structure) and stop
working, while below this the reaction is too slow — 30–40 °C is
the optimum**. And the yeast itself: it supplies the **enzymes**,
the biological catalysts, without which the sugar would not react
at all.
:::

:::did-you-know
The sucrose → glucose + fructose step hides an isomer surprise:
glucose and fructose have the *same* molecular formula (C₆H₁₂O₆)
but different structures — structural isomers, exactly as propan-1-ol
and propan-2-ol are in the alcohol family. The yeast's enzymes
are picky about which of the pair they process, which is part of
why the biochemistry takes many steps.
:::

:::misconception
"Fermentation eventually makes pure ethanol if you leave it long
enough." It never does: **yeast is killed by more than about 15%
alcohol**, so the reaction self-limits far below purity — the
product is very impure ethanol that needs fractional distillation
afterwards. Purity is the trade-off for fermentation's gentle,
renewable conditions; the hydration route buys purity with energy.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the glucose-to-ethanol equation with states? Can you
state the four fermentation conditions (raw material, temperature,
catalyst, atmosphere)? Can you *explain* both the anaerobic
requirement and the 30–40 °C window in enzyme language? Can you
say why fermentation caps at ~15% and what fixes it? Four yeses
and 4.32C's fermentation half plus all of 4.33C are yours.
:::

sections.title: Making ethanol by the hydration of ethene
sections.markdown:
The second industrial route comes straight out of the previous
lesson: ethanol is also made by reacting ethene with steam — a
process known as **[[hydration]]** (u4:c25, where the reaction made
its first appearance as an addition reaction of the alkenes). Now
it returns wearing its industrial hat, converting
ethene into [[ethanol]]:

CH₂=CH₂(g) + H₂O(g) → CH₃CH₂OH(g)

The conditions triplet is fixed: **ethene and steam**, a temperature
of about **300 °C**, a pressure of about **60–70 atmospheres**, and
a **phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) [[catalyst]]**. Only a small proportion of
the ethene reacts on each pass; the ethanol produced is condensed
as a liquid and the unreacted ethene is recycled through the
process — the recycle loop is what makes an inefficient single-pass
conversion industrially viable.

The reaction type deserves its own flag, because it is the same
addition chemistry the alkenes taught: this is an addition
reaction — the water is added to the ethene without removing
anything. No by-product leaves; the double bond is consumed; the
atoms all end up in one molecule of ethanol. Contrast that with
fermentation (Section 6), which *produces* carbon dioxide as a
co-product — one route adds everything it starts with, the other
splits a molecule and emits gas.

:::key-point
Hydration of ethene: ethene + steam, about 300 °C, about 60–70
atmospheres, phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) catalyst. It is an addition
reaction — the water adds to the ethene without removing anything
— and the unreacted ethene is recycled through the process.
:::

:::exam-hint
The hydration conditions are among the most examined triplets in
the course — deploy them verbatim: **steam, ~300 °C, ~60–70
atmospheres, phosphoric acid catalyst**. If asked to *describe two
conditions*, any two of the four (temperature, pressure, catalyst,
steam) earn the marks, but each must be specific — "high
temperature" alone is not; "about 300 °C" is. And name the
catalyst properly: **phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄**.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydration and fermentation differ only in speed." They differ in
nearly everything examinable: feedstock (petrochemical ethene vs
plant sugars), energy profile (forced conditions vs room-warm),
product purity (high vs very impure, capped at ~15%), reaction
type (addition vs enzymatic decomposition emitting CO₂), and
renewability (finite crude oil vs renewable crops). The
comparison section (Section 8) turns this contrast into a table —
but the table is only memorable once you know the two routes
individually.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the hydration equation with state symbols and name
the catalyst with its formula? Can you state all four process
conditions? Can you say why the reaction is classified as addition
and what the recycle loop is for? Four yeses and the petrochemical
route is banked.
:::

sections.title: Comparing the two methods of producing ethanol
sections.markdown:
Two routes, one product — and the comparison is the examinable
part. The table sets fermentation against the hydration of ethene
across five axes; learn it row by row, because "compare the two
methods" items pull directly from it.

| | Fermentation | Hydration of ethene |
|---|---|---|
| Use of resources | Uses **renewable** resources: sugar beet or sugar cane, corn and other starchy materials | Uses **finite, non-renewable** resources: once all the oil has been consumed, there won't be any more |
| Type of process | A **batch process**: everything is mixed together in a reaction vessel and left for several days; that batch is then removed and a new reaction is set up. Inefficient | A **continuous flow process**: a stream of reactants is constantly passed over the catalyst. More efficient than a batch process |
| Rate of reaction | Slow, taking several days for each batch | Quick |
| Quality of product | Produces **very impure** ethanol (capped at ~15% by the yeast) which needs further processing by fractional distillation | Produces **much purer** ethanol |
| Reaction conditions | Gentle temperatures and atmospheric pressure | High temperatures and pressures, requiring a high input of energy |

The vocabulary is itself examinable: a **[[batch-process]]** runs
discrete lots — mix, wait days, empty, repeat — while a
**[[continuous-process]]** flows reactants over the catalyst
without stopping, which is why it wins on efficiency and rate. And
the purity gap traces back to the biology: fermentation's yeast
ceiling means every litre needs **[[fractional-distillation]]**
afterwards, while hydration distils nothing biological and recycles
its own unreacted feedstock.

The strategic footnote is the future. At the moment, countries
with easy access to crude oil produce ethanol mainly from ethene —
but one day there will be no oil remaining. At that point, the
production of ethanol from sugar and starch provides an alternative
route to many of the organic chemicals we need: the renewable
route's gentle, slow, impure chemistry is the insurance policy
against the petrochemical route's finite feedstock.

:::key-point
Fermentation wins on resources (renewable, gentle conditions) and
loses on rate (days per batch), purity (very impure, ~15% yeast
ceiling, needs fractional distillation) and process type
(inefficient batch). Hydration wins on rate (quick), purity (much
purer) and process type (continuous flow) and loses on resources
(finite crude oil) and energy (high temperature and pressure).
:::

:::exam-hint
Comparison items are mark-scheme-row items: answer in the table's
own axes — resources, process type, rate, quality, conditions —
and quote the label words (**renewable/finite**, **batch/continuous
flow**, **impure/purer**, **gentle/high energy**). "Fermentation
is natural so it's better" is not a comparison; "fermentation uses
renewable sugar crops whereas hydration consumes finite crude oil"
is. And when the question asks for an *advantage of fermentation*,
reach for the resources row first — it is the row that never
flips.
:::

:::misconception
"The continuous process is better, so industry must always choose
hydration." Better *at what*? Hydration wins on speed and purity
but depends entirely on crude oil — a feedstock with an expiry
date. Countries without oil (Brazil is the standard example)
already prefer fermentation, and the textbook's own footnote makes
the long-run point: when the oil runs out, the batch process
becomes the only one left standing.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you reproduce all five comparison rows with the label words?
Can you define batch and continuous flow in one sentence each? Can
you trace fermentation's impurity back to the yeast ceiling and
name the purification fix? Three yeses and the comparison is
exam-ready.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 26 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete [[alcohol]] story. The family is defined
by the –OH functional group on a saturated chain (4.29C); its four
named members — methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol — come
with the draw-and-name discipline and the propan-1-ol/propan-2-ol
[[isomer]] distinction (4.30C); and ethanol, the family's
representative, does three oxidations — burning (Section 3),
microbial souring (Section 4), and the dichromate(VI) reflux that
turns orange to green (Section 5) — all landing on the same
product, [[ethanoic-acid]] (4.31C). Its two industrial routes,
[[fermentation]] (enzymes, ~30 °C, anaerobic — with the *why* of
each condition, 4.32C + 4.33C) and [[hydration]] (addition, H₃PO₄,
300 °C, 60–70 atm, making [[ethanol]]), close the chapter in a
five-row comparison.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you draw the four alcohols with the O–H bond shown? Can
you run all three oxidations — reagents, conditions, colour change
where there is one, product? Can you write the three key equations

The question bank for this chapter trains a predictable set of
shapes, so rehearse the moves rather than the answers. Drawing
items open the set: structural formulae for named alcohols,
displayed formulae with the O–H bond explicit, and naming from
condensed structures. Bonding items then ask for a dot-and-cross
diagram of ethanol — the covalent model (u1:c08) applied at a
functional group. Conditions items follow: two conditions of the
catalytic hydration, then the fermentation trio (yeast, 30–40 °C,
absence of air) with each condition *explained* in the Section 6
language, plus the Brazil economics. Equation items close the set:
the complete combustion of ethanol, the glucose-to-ethanol
conversion, the dichromate oxidation with [O] and its orange-to-
green observation, and a finishing item that runs ethanol
backwards to ethene — the dehydration completion — by supplying
the missing product. The shapes are the chapter; the alcohol names
are just costumes.

:::exam-hint
Two mark-dense habits for this bank. In oxidation items, the
product is always **ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH** — name it with its
formula, and pair the [O] shorthand with the named oxidising agent
in prose. In explanation items, mechanisms beat adjectives: "the
enzymes denature above 40 °C" earns, "it's too hot" does not. And
in any "state two conditions" item, take them verbatim from the
process boxes — specific numbers and named catalysts are what the
mark scheme stores.
:::

:::misconception
"The question bank rewards knowing the printed answers." It
rewards knowing the *chemistry* — the same oxidation can be asked
about through a different alcohol, the same comparison through a
different axis, the same fermentation through a different raw
material. This lesson trained the transferable routines: the
three-slice name decode, the O–H drawing discipline, the
reagents-conditions-observation-product structure for oxidations,
the row-wise comparison method. Run the method and the costume
does not matter.
:::

:::summary
- **The functional group (4.29C)**: alcohols contain –OH
  covalently bonded to a carbon chain; "alcohol" in everyday
  speech is ethanol, one member of the homologous series.
- **Drawing and naming (4.30C)**: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol
  CH₃CH₂OH, propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, butan-1-ol
  CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH; displayed formulae must show the O–H bond;
  propanol/butanol are acceptable names; the locant reports the
  –OH position and generates propan-1-ol/propan-2-ol isomers.
- **Three oxidations (4.31C)**: burning in air (complete
  combustion, C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)); microbial
  oxidation by air + microorganisms (wine → vinegar, ethanoic
  acid CH₃COOH); heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute
  sulfuric acid under reflux (orange → green, Cr³⁺, [O]
  shorthand: CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O).
- **Fermentation (4.32C + 4.33C)**: yeast enzymes convert glucose
  C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ at ~30 °C, anaerobic; no air because
  aerobic enzymes make CO₂ + water instead; 30–40 °C because the
  protein enzymes denature above ~40 °C and stall below; capped
  at ~15% alcohol (yeast dies), purified by fractional
  distillation (ethanol 78 °C vs water 100 °C).
- **Hydration (4.32C)**: ethene + steam, ~300 °C, ~60–70 atm,
  phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) catalyst; an addition reaction; recycle
  loop for the unreacted ethene.
- **The comparison**: renewable/batch/slow/impure/gentle vs
  finite/continuous/quick/purer/high-energy — and the long-run
  case for the renewable route when oil runs out.
:::

- draw and name all four alcohols, with the O–H bond explicit, and

- write the complete-combustion equation for ethanol with state

- describe all three oxidations — route, agents, observation,

- define fermentation, write the glucose equation, and *explain*

- state the hydration conditions verbatim with the catalyst's

- reproduce the five-row comparison with the label words, and say

:::
